reference.source: Hand surgery and sports medicine references
clinicalPearls: The triangular fibrocartilage complex stabilises the distal radioulnar joint and cushions the ulnar wrist, and its injury causes ulnar-sided wrist pain
Symptoms include ulnar wrist pain worse with rotation and gripping, clicking and sometimes distal radioulnar joint instability
Injuries are broadly traumatic or degenerative, the latter associated with positive ulnar variance and ulnar impaction
The fovea sign, with tenderness in the soft spot between the ulnar styloid and flexor carpi ulnaris, supports the diagnosis
MRI, and definitively wrist arthroscopy, characterise the tear and its location
Peripheral traumatic tears in the vascular zone can heal or be repaired, whereas central and degenerative tears are managed differently
reference.pathophysiology: The triangular fibrocartilage complex comprises the articular disc, ligaments and sheath that support the distal radioulnar joint and transmit load across the ulnar wrist. Acute injury from a fall onto the extended wrist or forceful rotation tears the complex, while chronic degenerative tears develop where excess ulnar length increases load on the disc (ulnar impaction). The peripheral portion is vascular and can heal, whereas the central avascular disc does not, which determines whether repair or debridement is appropriate. Loss of complex integrity may destabilise the distal radioulnar joint.
additionalDifferentials: Distal radioulnar joint instability of other cause
Hook of hamate fracture or pisotriquetral pathology
additionalInvestigations: Clinical examination including the fovea sign and distal radioulnar joint stability testing
MRI, ideally with arthrography, to image the tear
Wrist arthroscopy as the definitive diagnostic and often therapeutic tool
Comparison with the contralateral wrist for instability
redFlags: Progressive pain and weakness despite conservative care
Features suggesting an alternative structural injury
reference.prognosis: Many injuries respond to a period of immobilisation and rehabilitation; peripheral repairs and procedures to address ulnar impaction generally do well, whereas untreated instability can lead to chronic pain and arthritis.
pitfalls: Attributing ulnar wrist pain to a simple sprain and missing the diagnosis
Not recognising ulnar impaction as the driver of a degenerative tear
Expecting central avascular tears to heal like peripheral ones
management: Initial conservative management with wrist immobilisation in a splint or cast, activity modification and analgesia or a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug
Rehabilitation and physiotherapy to restore range of movement, grip strength and forearm rotation
Arthroscopic repair of peripheral traumatic tears in the vascular zone, which have healing potential
Arthroscopic debridement of irreparable central and degenerative tears
Ulnar shortening osteotomy or a wafer procedure to offload the disc in positive ulnar variance with ulnar impaction
Stabilise the distal radioulnar joint where the injury has caused instability
Refer to hand surgery for wrist arthroscopy, which serves as both definitive diagnosis and treatment
